Cosmology is the scientific study of the origin, evolution, structure, and large-scale properties of the universe [2]. It combines observations with theories from physics and astronomy [2]. The observable universe contains galaxies, stars, gas, dust, dark matter, radiation, and other forms of matter and energy [2]. Current measurements indicate the universe is approximately 13.8 billion years old [2]. The observable universe is larger than 13.8 billion light-years in radius because space has expanded while light was traveling [2]. The observable universe is defined as the region from which light or other signals have had time to reach us [2]. The entire universe may be larger than the observable universe, and whether it is finite or infinite is currently unknown [2, 4]. Cosmology studies the universe on scales much larger than individual galaxies [4]. The standard cosmological model is known as Lambda-CDM [4].

Observational cosmology uses astronomical measurements to test models of the universe [1]. Key datasets and methods include the cosmic microwave background, Type Ia supernovae for studying cosmic expansion, galaxy surveys to measure positions and redshifts, baryon acoustic oscillations as a standard ruler for cosmic distances, weak gravitational lensing to trace matter distribution, and galaxy clusters for information on structure growth and dark matter [1].

**Q: Whats the cosmos**

Answer:
Cosmology is the scientific study of the origin, evolution, structure, and large-scale properties of the universe [1]. It combines observations with theories from physics and astronomy [1]. Cosmology studies the universe on scales much larger than individual galaxies [2]. The standard cosmological model is called Lambda-CDM [2].

Details:
The observable universe contains galaxies, stars, gas, dust, dark matter, radiation, and other forms of matter and energy [1]. Current measurements indicate the universe is approximately 13.8 billion years old [1]. The observable universe is larger than 13.8 billion light-years in radius because space has expanded while light was traveling [1]. The observable universe is the region from which light or other signals have had time to reach us [1]. The entire universe may be much larger than the observable universe, and whether it is finite or infinite is not currently known [2]. The cosmic web is the large-scale network of filaments, clusters, groups, and voids containing galaxies [4]. Galaxies are major building blocks of the large-scale structure of the universe [5].

**Q: how are stars formed**

Answer:
Stars form within cold, dense regions of interstellar clouds, which are composed of gas and microscopic dust grains [1]. Gravity causes these dense regions to collapse, leading to an increase in density and temperature [1]. This collapsing material can form a protostar, which is a young stellar object that has not yet started stable hydrogen fusion [1]. As the protostar contracts, its rotation speeds up due to the conservation of angular momentum, and a circumstellar disk can form around it [1]. Planets can eventually form from the material in these disks [1].

Details:
The process begins in molecular clouds, where gravity overcomes internal support, causing collapse [2]. Turbulence and magnetic fields can also influence the structure and movement of gas within these clouds [3]. Star formation commonly occurs in the densest parts of molecular clouds, and a single cloud can produce multiple stars [3]. A protostar gains mass as material falls towards it, and the gravitational energy of this infalling material is converted into heat [3]. The protostellar stage concludes when the object begins stable hydrogen fusion [3].

COSMOLOGY
Cosmology is the scientific study of the origin, evolution, structure, and large-scale properties of the universe.
Modern cosmology combines observations with theories from physics and astronomy.
The observable universe contains galaxies, stars, gas, dust, dark matter, radiation, and other forms of matter and energy.
The universe is approximately 13.8 billion years old according to current measurements.
The observable universe is larger than 13.8 billion light-years in radius because space has expanded while light was traveling.
The observable universe is the region from which light or other signals have had time to reach us.
The entire universe may be much larger than the observable universe.
Whether the entire universe is finite or infinite is not currently known.

## OBSERVATIONAL COSMOLOGY

Observational cosmology uses astronomical measurements to test models of the universe.
The cosmic microwave background is one of its most important datasets.
Type Ia supernovae are used as distance indicators for studying cosmic expansion.
Galaxy surveys measure positions, redshifts, and properties of millions of galaxies.
Baryon acoustic oscillations provide a standard ruler for measuring cosmic distances.
Weak gravitational lensing traces the distribution of matter.
Galaxy clusters provide information about structure growth and dark matter.
